ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Geriatric Psychiatry Referral — Elizabeth I — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Primary care visit for low mood, poor sleep, poor appetite, and weight loss over three months after several bereavements

text.paragraph: Low mood, poor sleep, poor appetite, and 6 percent weight loss over three months in a 69-year-old woman after several bereavements, with PHQ-9 17, GDS-15 10, and a passive death wish. Please confirm the diagnosis and advise on treatment suited to an older adult and on her safety. [S]
Urgency: Soon, within two weeks; passive death wish without intent or plan, with a safety plan in place. [S]

list.item: Do you confirm a major depressive episode, as distinct from grief, and are there bipolar, psychotic, or cognitive features?
Which antidepressant, starting dose, and titration do you advise at 69, with low weight and a recent fall?
Which psychotherapy do you recommend, given her bereavements and her need for privacy?
Do you agree with the suicide-risk assessment and the safety plan?
How should her insomnia be treated now that diphenhydramine has stopped?
How long should treatment continue, and what would make you want to see her again?

text.paragraph: Ms. Tudor is a 69-year-old woman who has held a lifelong public office as head of state for more than forty years. Over three months she has had heavy low mood, loss of interest in music and riding, waking at 2 or 3 in the morning with about four hours of sleep, poor appetite, and a fall in weight from 55.9 to 52.4 kg (height 163 cm). Over the past two years several of those closest to her have died, including a former protégé and confidant after a bitter breach, and two friends of her own generation. On some mornings she wishes she would not wake; she has no active thoughts, intent, plan, or past self-harm, there are no firearms in her residence, and her maid keeps her medicines. A collaborative safety plan with the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline was made today. PHQ-9 17 (item 9 scored 1), GDS-15 10, MoCA 27. She has been taking over-the-counter diphenhydramine for sleep for six weeks; it was stopped today. Her upper partial denture is loose and chewing is painful. She stumbled and fell boarding a boat three weeks ago, bruising her shins. Blood count, metabolic panel, calcium, albumin, TSH, vitamin B12, and folate were sent today. She is very concerned about privacy and asks that her care stay within the clinic [S]

list.item: Heavy-hearted, sleeping about four hours a night, with no appetite, and her clothes are loose; she sometimes wishes she would not wake up. [S]
She fears that any word of her illness would leak and unsettle the country, and does not want to be seen as unfit for her office. [S]
Chewing is painful with her old partial denture, so she eats soft food and little of it. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Elizabeth was born at Greenwich on 7 September 1533 (Julian calendar; 17 September 1533 in the proleptic Gregorian calendar), the daughter of Henry VIII and his second wife, Anne Boleyn. [D]
Her mother, Anne Boleyn, was executed in 1536, when Elizabeth was two; her father, Henry VIII, reigned until 1547. [D]
She succeeded her half-sister Mary I on Mary's death in November 1558 and never married. [D]

In October 1562, aged 29, she fell ill at Hampton Court with a fever that turned to smallpox. On 15 October she wrote that a hot fever prevented her writing more; the Spanish ambassador reported that she lost her speech and was thought lost, that the eruption appeared in the night, and that she then improved. The court feared for the succession, and she recovered. [D]

Lady Sidney, who nursed her through the smallpox, caught it and was scarred for life; the court chronology states that, unlike the Queen, she was scarred. A medal struck for the Queen's recovery shows her face unblemished. [D]
A German visitor who saw her at Greenwich in August 1598, in her 65th year, described her face as fair but wrinkled and her teeth as black, a defect he attributed to the English use of sugar. [D]
On 25 February 1601 (Julian) the Earl of Essex, once her favourite, was executed at the Tower after his rising. [D]
Through 1602 court letters describe an ache in her arm that later spread to her side and hip; in September observers wrote that her health was very good and that she hunted and rode often. [D]
In December 1602 (Julian) she strained her foot leaving a dinner at her secretary's new house and, refusing help, stumbled and fell entering her barge, bruising her shins, which soon healed. [D]

On 27 December 1602 (Julian), her godson Sir John Harington wrote that she now bore show of human infirmity: he had found her in a most pitiable state, she wept at the memory of the Irish war in which he had served with the Earl of Essex, she said she was past her relish for his verses, and she told him that her bodily meat did not suit her and that she had eaten only one ill-tasted cake since the night before. [D]

list.item: Low mood, sleeplessness (about four hours a night), poor appetite, and unintended loss of 3.5 kg (6 percent) over three months, after bereavements and in a demanding public role; under evaluation for depression and medical causes: active, confirmed [S]
Partial loss of teeth with an ill-fitting upper partial denture and painful chewing, contributing to poor intake: active, confirmed [S]
One fall in the past year (a stumble boarding a boat, with bruised shins) and low body weight; fall risk: active, confirmed [S]

Workup for medical causes of low mood and weight loss: blood count, metabolic panel, calcium, albumin, TSH, vitamin B12, and folate; MoCA cognitive screen; medication review (stop the over-the-counter diphenhydramine sleep aid); dental examination; age-appropriate cancer screening confirmed up to date. Guideline: APA Clinical Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Depression Across Three Age Cohorts (2019); VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Major Depressive Disorder (2022); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, depression, bipolar, and mood disorders monograph (2026); American Geriatrics Society 2023 Updated AGS Beers Criteria for Potentially Inappropriate Medication Use in Older Adults (2023) [S]

Suicide-risk assessment and collaborative safety plan: warning signs, coping steps, people to contact, the clinic number, and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline; medicines kept by her maid; safety reviewed at every visit. Guideline: VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for Assessment and Management of Patients at Risk for Suicide (2024); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, depression, bipolar, and mood disorders monograph (2026) [S]

Sleep: stop diphenhydramine; cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (sleep window, stimulus control, a fixed rising time, no long naps, and worry time early in the evening); no benzodiazepines, Z-drugs, or sedating antihistamines. Guideline: American Geriatrics Society 2023 Updated AGS Beers Criteria for Potentially Inappropriate Medication Use in Older Adults (2023); Management of Chronic Insomnia Disorder in Adults: A Clinical Practice Guideline From the American College of Physicians (2016) [S]

Nutrition: three small meals and two snacks a day, an oral nutrition supplement twice a day, weight at every visit, and a dental review for the painful partial denture. Guideline: APA Clinical Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Depression Across Three Age Cohorts (2019); VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Major Depressive Disorder (2022); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, depression, bipolar, and mood disorders monograph (2026) [S]

Falls: Timed Up and Go and orthostatic blood pressure now and again if an antidepressant is started, since SSRIs raise fall risk in older adults; home safety review with her staff; an exercise class for balance and strength. Guideline: American Geriatrics Society 2023 Updated AGS Beers Criteria for Potentially Inappropriate Medication Use in Older Adults (2023); Falls Prevention in Community-Dwelling Older Adults: Interventions (2024) [S]

Measurement-based care: PHQ-9 at every visit and at least monthly and GDS-15 monthly; if an SSRI is started, a sodium check two to four weeks later; continue any treatment that works for at least six to twelve months after remission. Guideline: APA Clinical Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Depression Across Three Age Cohorts (2019); VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Major Depressive Disorder (2022); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, depression, bipolar, and mood disorders monograph (2026); American Geriatrics Society 2023 Updated AGS Beers Criteria for Potentially Inappropriate Medication Use in Older Adults (2023) [S]

Privacy: chart access restricted to her care team, appointments at the end of the clinic day, results given in person, and nothing released without her written consent. Guideline: APA Clinical Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Depression Across Three Age Cohorts (2019); VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Major Depressive Disorder (2022); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, depression, bipolar, and mood disorders monograph (2026) [S]
Referral to geriatric psychiatry, Gideon Rasmussen-Hale, MD, ordered 1603-01-12 [S]
